title: Samantabhadra's promise (Kern ch. 26)
hook: the bodhisattva of practice promises to protect those who keep the sutra

segments.voice: Yesterday, two princes walked on the air until their father asked who had taught them. Your line: the sons led the king. Who younger showed you something? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-three.

The Lotus Sutra is nearly over when, in chapter twenty-six, a late guest arrives from a world far to the east, with a great company behind him. His name is Samantabhadra. He bows, and he asks the Buddha a practical question, the kind someone asks near the end of a long meeting. After you are gone, how will people get hold of this teaching? What does it take? Today: Samantabhadra's promise.
screen: `A LATE GUEST FROM THE EAST.` → `HIS NAME IS SAMANTABHADRA.` → `HOW WILL PEOPLE KEEP THIS?`

segments.voice: The Buddha answers with a short list. Roughly: be held in the care of the Buddhas, plant roots of goodness, join the company of those set on the path, and turn the mind toward freeing all beings. Then Samantabhadra makes his promise, and it's surprisingly concrete. Whoever keeps this sutra, he says, I will guard. When that person walks and turns the teaching over in their mind, I'll come riding a white elephant with six tusks, and stand before them. When they sit and reflect on it, I'll come again. And if they forget a line of it, even one word, I'll be there to give it back. He adds protective spells, so that nothing harmful can find an opening. The Buddha praises him for it. Look at what the promise is attached to. Not to being clever, not to being finished. To keeping: reading, remembering, turning the words over while walking. The protection follows the practice, step for step. In the traditions that honor him, Samantabhadra is the bodhisattva of practice, of vows actually carried out. And this is the week's last day, so look back at what the end of the Lotus has been saying. Spells to guard those who keep it. The Medicine King's offering. Gadgadasvara in many forms. Guanyin hearing every cry, and a chapter chanted on its own. Two sons leading a king. And now a bodhisattva on a white elephant, promising to walk beside whoever keeps it. Week after week the Lotus has said: this is precious. This week it said: and you won't be left alone with it.
screen: `HOW TO GET HOLD OF THE TEACHING.` · `A WHITE ELEPHANT WITH SIX TUSKS.` · `A FORGOTTEN LINE, GIVEN BACK.` · `THE PROTECTION FOLLOWS THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `KEPT AND PROTECTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: keep one practice faithfully. Settle, and feel the breath come in and go out. Now choose one small thing you already do, or would like to. This sit. A line you say in the morning. A walk without your phone. Watering a plant. Keep it small enough that you could do it tomorrow on a bad day. Hold it in mind the way you'd hold a promise you made to a friend. You don't need to promise forever. Just tomorrow. Then rest, and let the breath do the keeping for now. The bell holds the time.
Samantabhadra's promise. To come, on a white elephant, to anyone who keeps the sutra, and to give back any line they forget. Today's word.

Your line: kept and protected. Today, do the one small practice you chose, even if the day goes badly. Spells, the Medicine King, many forms, the universal gate, the king and his sons, the promise: that was the week. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: In East Asian Mahayana traditions Samantabhadra is honored as the bodhisattva of practice and vows, and temple images show him seated on a white elephant; communities that keep the Lotus Sutra read this chapter as his pledge to protect them.

fork.setup: you're Samantabhadra. the Lotus is almost done, and the Buddha won't be in the world forever. what do you offer?
options: to write the sutra's final chapter yourself.
to guard anyone who keeps it, and give back the lines they forget.
to carry the sutra away to a safer world.
fork.reveal: he promises to come on a white elephant to whoever keeps the sutra, walking or sitting, and to restore any word they forget.

original.note: Sanskrit: the name of the bodhisattva who rides the white elephant in this chapter.

trapdoor: what you thought: a guardian angel story.
what it means: a bodhisattva promises to stand beside anyone who keeps the sutra, and to give back any line they forget.
what a scholar hears: the protection is tied to keeping, walking and reflecting; this is why traditions name Samantabhadra the bodhisattva of practice.

notes: Chapter paraphrased from Kern (1884) ch. 26, not quoted. Confirm the Buddha's short list of conditions (Kern: four qualities). 'Four' is left out of the voice on purpose.
'A white elephant with six tusks': confirm Kern's wording in ch. 26.
Promise to appear when the keeper walks and when they sit, and to restore forgotten words: confirm against Kern.
'Bodhisattva of practice' is the outline's description and an East Asian reception; confirm. howItsDone says temple images show him on a white elephant; confirm the phrasing.
